The Secret · Byron Preiss, 1982 · Casque 5 of 12

Chicago —
The First Casque

We at the Voynich Times spend a lot of our days on hunts that never ended. This one did — and fast. In 1982, Byron Preiss buried twelve casques in twelve North American cities, each holding a key that could be redeemed for a birthstone. Chicago's was the first ever found: three Chicago teenagers read a painting and Verse 12 as walking directions, followed them through Grant Park step by step, and dug the casque up in 1983, a year after the book appeared. We've walked that verse ourselves (well, on paper, at least) and it still stings that three kids beat us to it!

One casque of twelve. This dossier is a single find from The Secret (1982) — the whole story of the book, the twelve burials, and the nine still in the ground lives on the hub: The Secret: A Treasure Hunt ↗

Section 1 · Image 5

The Painting

Palencar hid the whole walk in this one picture. The tower and the fountain figure and the outline of Illinois name the city (the state outline is reversed — Palencar mirrored it), the horseman waits up on the castle wall for the corner of Congress where you'll meet him in bronze, and the fence drawn across that same wall is the confirmation — the pattern your eyes have to match when you're standing on the spot, wondering if you've finally got it right. The grid references in the table are the community's, worked out on the Quest4Treasure wiki.

Section 2 · Verse 12

The Verse

Read it the way the boys did — as walking directions. South along Michigan Avenue, east into Grant Park at Congress, then northeast to Lincoln and northwest into the grove, and the whole hunt is over in fifteen lines.

Where M and B are set in stone And to Congress, R is known L sits and left Beyond his shoulder Is the Fair Folks' Treasure holder The end of ten by thirteen Is your clue Fence and fixture Central too For finding jewel casque Seek the sounds Of rumble Brush and music Hush.
VERSE 12 · FROM THE SECRET (1982)
“Where M and B are set in stone”

Mozart and Beethoven, engraved on Orchestra Hall (Symphony Center), 220 S. Michigan Ave. Preiss's own gloss — but disputed; the community alternative is “Man and Beast” (the Bowman and his horse). Both readings put you at the same corner. See Disputes.

“And to Congress, R is known”

R = Roosevelt: Roosevelt University's Auditorium Building, Michigan Ave at Congress (now Ida B. Wells Dr).

“L sits and left / Beyond his shoulder”

L = Lincoln: Saint-Gaudens' Seated Lincoln, Grant Park. Approached from the Bowman, you face him looking north; left past his shoulder aims you northwest into the grove.

“Is the Fair Folks' / Treasure holder”

The Art Institute of Chicago — built for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, holder of treasures, one block west.

“The end of ten by thirteen / Is your clue”

Two planted tree lines — one of ten, one of thirteen — crossing in the grove; the casque at the end/intersection. By 1983 the city had cut a tree from each row, breaking the count until Preiss told the finders to adjust for missing trees. Orientation disputed — see Disputes.

Our drawing, after theirs: thirteen trees across the top, ten down the side, the two lines meeting at an open corner at the grove's northwest — the hole, in the clear the way the finders' map draws it, not under a tree — with one tree already cut from each row, the gap Preiss told the boys to count before the numbers would line up. The finders' original map survives in ABC7 Chicago's February 2018 segment and on the community wiki's Verse 12 page, which also carries a 2002 aerial of the corner. Gasiorowski remembered the counts swapped — ten across, thirteen down.

“Fence and fixture / Central too”

The arched fence (drawn in the painting) + an electrical fixture/box on the bridge wall + Central = the Illinois Central tracks beside the site.

“Seek the sounds / Of rumble”

Trains on the IC tracks, directly beside and under the Jackson bridge.

“Brush and music”

Brush = the Art Institute (paint). Music = the Petrillo Band Shell in Grant Park.

“Hush.”

Unresolved Best community guess: the digging was in a very public place.

Section 3 · Grant Park, Chicago

The Walk

Seven pins, and they run in the order the solve runs — the painting names the city, the verse walks you down Michigan Avenue, and one fencepost in a grove ends it. The map is our own; tap a pin and it will tell you where you're standing. Every card below carries its own Google Map and Street View links, so you can walk the whole thing from your chair (the digging, happily, is already done).

The Secret — Chicago (Image 5 / Verse 12) — our own map: the found casque and the six solve steps.

1Stage A · City lock

Chicago Water Tower

Image clue: the windmill tower, upper right of the painting

806 N. Michigan Ave. The castle-like limestone tower (1869), drawn in the painting as a Dutch windmill — the first thing Eric Gasiorowski spotted, too, before anyone had walked a step. Coordinates 41.89719, −87.62436.

2Stage A · City lock + park anchor

Fountain of the Great Lakes

Image clue: the water-pouring woman — Lake Michigan

Art Institute South Garden. Lorado Taft carved five women for the five Great Lakes, and the one pouring from her bowl in the painting is Lake Michigan — she is the painting's way of walking you into the park. Coordinates 41.87875, −87.62340. (Art Institute of Chicago ↗)

Orchestra Hall (Symphony Center)

“Where M and B are set in stone”

220 S. Michigan Ave. Mozart and Beethoven, engraved in stone over the ballroom windows — Preiss's own reading of M and B (the old guard swears it's Man and Beast; that argument is in Disputes). Coordinates 41.87903, −87.62491.

Roosevelt University — Auditorium Building

“And to Congress, R is known”

430 S. Michigan Ave at Congress (now Ida B. Wells Dr). R = Roosevelt, and the Auditorium Building stands on Congress itself — the verse names the street and the building answers to it. You're at the park's gate. Coordinates 41.87590, −87.62510.

The Bowman, Congress Plaza

Image clue: the horseman silhouette on the castle

Meštrović's Native American rider, sculpted deliberately with empty hands — the Bowman with no bow — standing where Congress enters Grant Park. Coordinates 41.87598, −87.62348.

Seated Lincoln, Grant Park

“L sits and left / Beyond his shoulder”

Saint-Gaudens' “Abraham Lincoln: The Head of State.” Stand in front of him and look left, beyond his shoulder, and the line runs northwest into the grove between Lincoln and the Jackson Dr wall — the verse's last pointer before the trees take over. Coordinates 41.87729, −87.62154.

7Stage C · The pinpoint — steps 4–6

THE DIG SITE — Found 1983 ◆

“The end of ten by thirteen” · “Fence and fixture / Central too” · “rumble”

Beside the Illinois Central (now Metra) tracks, just south of the E. Jackson Dr bridge wall: the 10×13 tree grid, the arched fence from the painting, an electrical fixture on the wall — and twelve inches down, the box. Everything the verse promised, in one corner of one grove. Coordinates 41.87844, −87.62244 (±50 m — see Disputes).

Google Map ↗Street View ↗

Field note: the Street View panorama shot from above the dig spot appears to show a casque (or a replica someone placed there). The Art Institute itself — the “Fair Folks' treasure holder” — stands at 111 S. Michigan Ave (41.87958, −87.62366), immediately north of the fountain garden. The Petrillo Band Shell (“music”) is an ambient reference, not a walked waypoint, and is not pinned.

Section 4 · 1983

The Dig

The solve and the recovery were two different fights. The boys had the right park and the right corner relatively early; the tree grid nearly beat them.

1 · The early digs

Working from the painting and verse, Gasiorowski, Wrobel, and James dug roughly a half-dozen holes across Grant Park without success.

2 · They wrote to Preiss

The finders sent Preiss photographs of where they'd been looking. He told them they were on the right track — and sent back a photograph of the precise burial location, the freshly patted earth as he'd left it. (Preiss's photo-assist was a one-time product of 1983; the rules of engagement changed after Chicago.)

3 · The tree call

Wrobel got Preiss on the phone and walked him through their process. At the end Preiss asked what they made of “10 × 13.” The counts didn't add up — not 10 in one row, not 13 in the other. Preiss “chuckled” and told them to recount and adjust for any trees that might be missing. The city had cut down one tree in each row — with the gaps counted as positions, the lines suddenly lined up (nearly a year of digging, settled in the end by counting trees that weren't there).

4 · The final hole

Even lined up, the big final hole missed: the box was further to the side than they thought. Frustrated, one of them threw a shovel into the hole; dirt slid off the side wall and exposed the Plexiglas box, its top only about 12 inches below the surface.

5 · The redemption

Inside the ceramic casque was a small key. Mailed to Preiss, it was exchanged for the emerald. The finders kept the hand-painted ceramic casque itself, valued at $500 in 1983.

“Without the information made available to us, the site would never have been found due to the change in the count of the trees. We could have finished the hunt almost a year earlier.”

— ERIC GASIOROWSKI, FINDER'S WRITE-UP [4]

Who was actually at the dig

The credited finders are Eric Gasiorowski, Rob Wrobel, and David James, and the three were to split the find three ways. Two more things from the community record:

· David James was not present on the day of the discovery, though he is counted a finder.

· Danny Rosenbach, a friend of the group, is the one who physically discovered/uncovered the casque in the hole (per the Quest4Treasure reading of the Tribune account).

Section 6 · Still argued

Disputes & Open Questions

Some of this is still argued about, and where the sources disagree we print both versions and leave them side by side. The site today: the trees are gone (the east–west line is 80% cut; only 3 of the original 13 remain in the north–south line), and the fencepost at the spot no longer carries its arched “halo” section. The solve is a historical reconstruction, not re-walkable end-to-end.

Uncertainty · ±50 m

Where exactly was it?

Two coordinates stand in the record, ~37 m apart, both inside the finders' own spread of recollections. Gasiorowski's marker photo puts the spot much closer to the Jackson wall than the Street View panorama's apparent casque/replica. The record doesn't justify picking one over the other, so both numbers stay.

Our map pin (geocode of 196 E. Jackson Dr)41.87844, −87.62244
Wiki's final location [1]41.878116, −87.622337
Disputed

“M and B” — Mozart & Beethoven vs. Man and Beast

The wiki relays Preiss's own answer (Mozart and Beethoven, carved on Orchestra Hall). The Quest4Treasure old guard insists M and B stands for Man and Beast — the Bowman (man) and his horse (beast) — “not Mozart and Beethoven as Mr. Preiss has said.” Both readings put you at the same corner of Michigan Ave, which is why the solve survives the dispute. Status: unresolved — Preiss said one thing, the old guard insists on the other, and the corner doesn't care.

Disputed

Which row was 10, and which was 13?

Gasiorowski's write-up says 10 east–west, 13 north–south. The kids' own hand-drawn map (glimpsed in the 2018 ABC7 footage) labels the east–west dots “13” and the north–south dots “10” — the reverse. It may be fallible memory, or green-ink labels added later by an unknown hand. Status: unresolved, and now unverifiable — the trees are gone.

Open

Exact find date

Only the year (1983) and the Tribune's August 9, 1983 coverage are firm. Some publisher reissue blurbs say 1984. That is a publisher error.

Open

“Hush.”

No agreed reading. Best community guess: the digging was in a very public place.

Open

Collar numerals & the ear-flap symbol

The “2” and “88” on the painting's collar, and the symbol at the hat's ear flap, remain unassigned.

Field notes

If visiting: the site is public parkland beside an active rail corridor — view from the Jackson Dr sidewalk / Street View side; the tracks are Metra Electric / South Shore, live and fenced. Nothing to dig: the casque is recovered, and the tree grid that proved the spot no longer exists. The single best pre-visit artifact is Gasiorowski's marker photo (his copy of the book on the ground at the dig spot, facing west toward the fence and tracks), hosted on the wiki solution page [1].
